title: Sort an array of 0's 1's and 2's
stepTitle: Solve Problems on Arrays [Easy -> Medium -> Hard]
category: Solve Problems on Arrays [Easy -> Medium -> Hard]
problemStatement: Sort an array containing only 0s, 1s and 2s in one pass, in-place.
intuition: Only three distinct values exist, so you can maintain three regions — settled 0s, settled 1s, unknown, settled 2s — and shrink the unknown region to nothing. This is Dijkstra's Dutch National Flag partition.

approaches.title: Brute: sort
approaches.idea: Ignores the fact that the value domain has size 3.
limitations: Comparison sort is strictly more than the problem needs

approaches.title: Better: counting sort (two passes)
limitations: Two passes; not allowed if the interviewer demands a single pass

approaches.title: Optimal: Dutch National Flag, one pass
approaches.dryRun:
a=[2,0,2,1,1,0] low=0 mid=0 high=5
a[0]=2 -> swap with high: [0,0,2,1,1,2] high=4
a[0]=0 -> swap low/mid: low=1 mid=1
a[1]=0 -> low=2 mid=2
a[2]=2 -> swap with a[4]: [0,0,1,1,2,2] high=3
a[2]=1 mid=3; a[3]=1 mid=4 > high -> stop
approaches.whyWorks: When you swap a 2 to the back you bring in an unexamined element, so mid must NOT advance. When you swap a 0 forward you bring in an already-examined 1, so mid may advance.

specialTechnique.title: Dutch National Flag
specialTechnique.body: Three-way partition around a pivot value. Same machinery powers 3-way quicksort on arrays with many duplicates.

edgeCases: Only two of the three values present
commonMistakes: Incrementing mid after swapping with high — the incoming element is unchecked
Looping while mid < high instead of mid <= high, leaving the last element unsorted
patternRecognition: Tiny value domain + in-place + single pass -> three-way partition
followUps: Partition around an arbitrary pivot (quicksort core)
Why does counting sort fail the "one pass" constraint?
interviewInsight: Say the loop invariant before you write the loop. The mid/high asymmetry is exactly what they are probing.
